newsitem.title: USA: Flooding Illinois rivers drive hundreds from homes.
newsitem.headline: Flooding Illinois rivers drive hundreds from homes.

text.p: Flooding rivers that spilled over miles of farmland forced hundreds of people out of their homes in northern Illinois on Monday, authorities said.

Extremely heavy rain and then snow that fell late last week sent the swollen Rock and Illinois Rivers over their banks and into homes and basements across northern Illinois. Hundreds of people in the hamlets of Erie and Hillsdale along the Rock River had to evacuate in the face of rising floodwaters.

"The town is surrounded by water -- there's only one way in and out," Ron Hanson, a spokesman for Whiteside County Emergency Management Agency, said of Erie, a town of 1,500 about 130 miles (210 km) west of Chicago.

Ice jams breaking apart upstream threatened to unleash a wall of water that could inundate the towns, Hanson said. The Rock River had spread to a width of two miles (3 km) of mostly rural farmland in some sections. Residents had filled 20,000 sandbags to try to protect homes and businesses.
Several Chicago suburbs affected by Friday's downpour were gradually drying out, although dozens of homes were still surrounded by standing water from overflowing tributaries.
Low-lying areas along the Illinois River in the centre of the state were also under water, with the river expected to crest this week a few feet above the level of Peoria's seawall, officials said.

Businesses and streets that lie near the riverbank could be flooded if the water spills over the seawall, and less-protected towns along the river may be inundated, Peoria's disaster services director Kay Harmon said. She said Peoria could see its worst flooding in eight years.

Downstream, where the Illinois River flows into the Mississippi north of St. Louis, disaster preparations were under way, including a plan to bulldoze a temporary dirt levee onto a highway in West Alton. But the latest prediction from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers lowered Wednesday's anticipated crest of the Mississippi by a couple of feet, easing fears.

"We're on guard," said Petra Haws, a spokeswoman for St. Charles County, Missouri. "Up North (on the Illinois River and other tributaries) they're going to crest later this week, so that means there's another wave of water coming this way."
